body:
This movie will very quickly draw criticism from fans of the much loved Schwarzenegger classic Predator, but I think it's going to get unnecessary hate for the wrong reasons.

Like most I have been a fan of this franchise for a long time. But it's had it's problems that originated from the second movie and after it, hitting it's lowest points at the AvP movies and the 2018 Shane Black helmed 'The Predator'

Director Dan Trachtenberg brought back some life into the franchise with the brilliant 'Prey' in a much more character driven picture. One of my worries with long running franchises wether it be this, Alien or even Terminator is that later installments tried to hard to replicate what made it special in the beginning, they often fail and the series become over familiar without bringing much expansion to the universe in which they are set.

For better or worse, this movie does what the series needed to not only stay relevant but to move forward, it's expanded on the characters and universe. And what's exiting about this director is that he rarely does the same thing twice. So for people worried that this derives to much from the Schwarzenegger original, then I think that worry later on may be altered. This director has now done two projects (3 if you count the animation) and there is nothing stopping him later on, bringing both his new vision plus the movie some fans were expecting together.

Sure this movie is not perfect, but little are, I think the change in tone may divide some fans but I think at least it shows us a glimpse into the Predator world and gives us a insight into their motivations, which I think it tells very well.

I think it only really let me down on two aspects, I think hiding away from the expected R rating is not something I want to see happen continuously, I would rather see it as more of a 18 rating. And some of the effects and designs are something more seen in something out of Star Wars than I would expect to see in this.

But I really enjoyed the story, and it's not a franchise killer for me that we see a different type of role for a Predator character. Sure it's not the first movie to turn what is expected to be a villian into the good guy, but I think it's pretty effective done this time around. Again, I don't want to see this in all future installments.

The effects were pretty great throughout as were the performances, especially by Elle Fanning who was terrific in her dual role.

But ultimately it's something I had a lot of fun with, and it was different, which is what franchises sometimes needs but they mostly avoid. Definitely exited to see what's in hold for the future, there is still a lot of life left in this franchise, which is more than I can say for a lot of the franchises I once loved.

Whose idea was it to turn Predator into a beat-for-beat Disney-style adventure film? This is Predator in name only. There is virtually none of the horror, tension, or atmosphere from the original. It feels like a cardboard cutout, generic kids movie. It may as well have been a Disney Channel original.

I could not believe they included every stereotype: the quirky, annoying sidekick who asks endless questions while traveling, the cutesy creature the audience is supposed to adore, the forced found-family dynamic, and the overtly evil villains with shallow motivations. It's seriously reminded me of like this straight to dvd kids movies my parents bought for me when I was a kid. Unbelievable.

In this film, the Predator becomes a superhero. And a superhero of the most banal character imaginable. The first half of the film may really intrigue you with its new approach to telling the story of this super-strong alien, where the humanoid must prove his hunting prowess to the father of the Yautja clan, who, among other things, kills his brother while he is saving the protagonist. Why does our Predator need to prove anything to his so-called father? It's unclear. I couldn't empathize with the Predator on the basis of human emotions because of his motives, which the director tried so hard to squeeze out through his relationship with the android from the Alien universe and another ugly alien trying to appear cute. He literally becomes good at the snap of a finger, simply because the plot requires it, since the third act has arrived. The idea is interesting, but as always, the execution is lousy, and don't be fooled by the fact that this is a 20th Century Studios film, because only one studio could take this approach.

I love the original Predator film and who doesn't. And the love was never just about our favourite muscle man Arnold. I actually loved the creature. For its time, it was an incredibly inventive design. Its imposing presence almost dwarfing Arnie, the sophisticated weaponry that shredded everything in an instant, the invisibility cloak, and finally the iconic face reveal. That film became the foundation for everything that followed.

But I never quite enjoyed the sequels and reboots. In fact, I skipped a few. Of the ones I did watch, I liked the first AVP (2004) and the more recent Prey (2022). Alien vs Predator was a lot of fun and gave us exciting backstory about the species and their hunting rituals. I wish that franchise had expanded further. Prey was a genuine surprise, placing a Predator into what felt like the 17th or 18th century and letting it collide with an entirely different kind of conflict. A terrific idea executed with finesse.

Badlands comes from the same team that made Prey, so the expectations were high. It is set centuries later in a dystopian future, and for the first time ever, a Predator is the protagonist. The film is under two hours and wastes no time. The opening minutes are terrific and hit you with great urgency.

Our hero Dek is a young Yautja (their species name) who is about to be eliminated for being weak and is seen as a disgrace to his clan. But Dek is a spirited fighter and refuses to accept this fate. After a great action sequence and a dramatic escape, he sets his plan in motion. He will travel to a dangerous planet and hunt a Kalisk, supposedly the most lethal creature out there. If he returns with its head as a trophy, he will redeem himself. The rest of the film follows this quest.

The world Dek enters is full of wildly imaginative creatures and some humanoids. Some help him, some become terrifying obstacles. Elle Fanning plays two humanoids, Tessa and Thea, and she brings a great presence to both roles, clearly having a lot of fun. The name of the company which has sent these humanoids to this planet is Weyland-Yutani Corporation (a company from the Alien franchise). This link clearly shows that the future Predator films could very well merge into the Aliens saga.

The creature design in Badlands is one of the most inventive I have seen in recent years. The Kalisk is nothing like the usual giant dragon or T-Rex derivative. I am tired of seeing Godzilla clones. This is something entirely new. And beyond the Kalisk, Dek encounters several fascinating species, each creatively designed.

The action choreography is another major win. The sequences are sharp, never overlong, and consistently entertaining. Visually, the film is stunning. From its landscapes to its tech to its creature work, it feels fresh and original. Dek himself is the most human-like Yautja we have ever seen. His proportions are closer to ours, and his emotional journey is surprisingly affecting. You can see him change as the story progresses.

The ending is satisfying yet leaves a wide window open for Dek's story to continue, and I genuinely hope it does. I have always been a fan of the Predator creature. But after this film, I now have a unique individual to root for, Dek.

Watch it if you enjoy action films with inventive creatures and a truly human story at the center.

Hey. Visually all there. But remember when Star Wars started throwing in gags? I mean here we go again. More pandering and less epic. And for what? Contrived relationships and nerfed villains. And yes we get it: "copy right copy right trademarked" did anyone else catch that? C'mon guys, I just want to watch a movie.
